title: Topics 7–8: mechanisms checkpoint
subtitle: An original 20-mark check with a separate feedback route
objective: Apply selected ideas about hormonal control, circulation and exchange, then use evidence to choose a precise next step.

sow.alignment: Summer C35 Paper 2 topic-assessment row. This is a teacher-authored 20-mark checkpoint on selected Topics 7–8, not an official Pearson paper, complete Paper 2 coverage or a source of GCSE grade predictions. Core insulin is included; Higher-only glucagon is not required.

priorLearning: Hormones travel in blood to responsive target tissues.
The heart forms two linked circulatory circuits.
Ventilation and diffusion have different mechanisms.
success: Explain an insulin response without confusing hormone and stored material.
Use vessel direction, pump calculations and exchange mechanisms accurately.
Review item evidence and identify one specific improvement.

vocabulary.meaning: Regulation of internal conditions within limits.
A pancreatic hormone involved in reducing raised blood glucose.
A vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
Volume pumped by one ventricle per unit time.
Movement of air into and out of the lungs.
Net movement of particles down a concentration gradient.

equipment: Shared source page, one selected checkpoint route, feedback page, pen and calculator.
Timer and teacher mark guidance; answers remain with the adult until independent work ends.
preparation: Print the shared page, one selected response route and the exit page. Routes are alternatives, not extra tasks.
Read the worked answers and note any constructed data before teaching.
Use the 18-minute independent window for Q1–Q5. All three routes carry the same 20 core marks. Record route and any reading, prompting or calculation support.
This is a check after a short recap. Do not present it as an unassisted baseline or use the score to predict a GCSE grade.
Keep teacher answers and live answer-reveal controls out of view during the checkpoint. Reveal feedback only after collecting or pausing responses.
safety: Paper and screen lesson; no human sampling, exercise test, breath holding, medicine handling or personal health disclosure.
practicalAlternative: All evidence is supplied. Use paper diagrams and cards, pointing, annotation or dictation if a device is unavailable.

misconceptions.claim: The hormone insulin becomes the glycogen store.
misconceptions.correction: Glucose is used to build glycogen; insulin is a signal.
misconceptions.check: Use Q1 to distinguish signal from response.

misconceptions.claim: An artery is defined by oxygen content.
misconceptions.correction: An artery carries blood away from the heart, including the pulmonary artery.

misconceptions.claim: Inhalation begins because lung pressure rises.
misconceptions.correction: Increasing thoracic volume lowers pressure below the surroundings, drawing air in.

misconceptions.claim: A checkpoint total is a GCSE grade.
misconceptions.correction: This small teacher-authored check samples selected content and records support.
misconceptions.check: Use item patterns to choose teaching, not a grade conversion.

access.supported: Same five core questions and marks, with chunked wording, a word bank and optional read-aloud. Record these supports alongside the result.
access.standard: Same five core questions and marks with independent explanations. Calculator access is allowed and recorded.
access.stretch: Same 20-mark core first. An optional unscored model-audit question follows if time permits; it does not change the score.
access.regulation: Offer solo or partner work, a quiet response, a pass and brief reset with clear re-entry. No forced disclosure or public performance.

slides.title: A precise checkpoint, then a useful next step
body: Five questions, 20 core marks.
Short recap first; 18 minutes for independent work.
slides.notes: Explain that this is original selected-topic practice after a recap. Record the chosen route and support. No grade prediction or public score ranking.

slides.title: Retrieve a route and a process
body: R1. What carries an endocrine hormone around the body?
R2. What is the difference between ventilation and diffusion?
slides.notes: R1 blood. R2 ventilation moves air through pressure changes; diffusion is net particle movement down a gradient. Accept spoken or pointed responses.

slides.title: Trace the hormone message
body: Gland releases a hormone into blood.
Responsive cells recognise the signal and change activity.
slides.notes: Think aloud through location → carrier → response. This general recap does not rehearse the checkpoint wording. Recognition explains why every cell does not respond identically.

visual.title: One message, three important locations
visual.description: Endocrine transport model: an endocrine gland releases a hormone into circulating blood; the hormone reaches tissues, but only appropriate target cells respond. Arrows show information/material transport, not a private gland-to-organ duct.

elements.text:
Endocrine gland
Hormone released
into blood

Target cells
Recognise signal
Change activity

The bloodstream distributes the signal.
Cell recognition helps determine the response.

slides.title: Read direction before oxygen content
body: An artery takes blood away from the heart.
Follow the lung circuit to test the definition.
slides.notes: Trace right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs. It carries relatively oxygen-poor blood away from the heart. Let pupils see how the vessel definition differs from its oxygen content.

visual.title: Two linked circuits, one continuous route
visual.description: Schematic double circulation: body→right heart→lungs→left heart→body. Blue-labelled paths carry relatively oxygen-poor blood; red-labelled paths carry relatively oxygen-rich blood. Colour is accompanied by text. The positions are not anatomical.

elements.text: Two linked circuits, one continuous route
Artery = away from heart; vein = towards heart.

slides.title: Volume and pressure explain ventilation
body: Inhalation increases volume and lowers pressure.
Quiet exhalation involves relaxation and recoil.
slides.notes: Trace one mechanical sequence. Distinguish the resulting airflow from diffusion across the alveolar barrier. This is a recap, not a breathing practical.

visual.title: Ventilation changes volume and pressure
visual.description: Two-panel schematic of quiet breathing. Inhalation: diaphragm contracts/flattens, ribs move up/out, thoracic volume rises and pressure falls below atmospheric pressure so air enters. Quiet exhalation: muscles relax and elastic recoil reduces volume, raising pressure so air leaves.

elements.text:
Diaphragm contracts/flattens
Volume rises; pressure falls
Air enters

Diaphragm relaxes; recoil
Volume falls; pressure rises
Air leaves

slides.title: Use an analogous calculation
body: W1. Model M: 60 beats/min × 50 mL/beat.
Model N: 80 beats/min × 50 mL/beat.
Calculate N after the teacher models M.
slides.notes: Model M = 3,000 mL/min = 3 L/min. Joint N = 4,000 mL/min = 4 L/min. Cancel beat units, then divide by 1,000. These are warm-up records, not checkpoint A/B.

visual.title: Warm-up only: model pump output
visual.description: Constructed recap data, separate from the checkpoint. M: 60 beats/min × 50 mL/beat = 3,000 mL/min = 3 L/min. N: 80 × 50 = 4,000 mL/min = 4 L/min.

slides.title: Challenge a pair of claims
body: W2. “All blood-carried hormones affect every cell equally.”
W3. “The pulmonary artery is a vein because its blood is oxygen-poor.”
slides.notes: W2 false: responsiveness/recognition matters. W3 false: it leaves the heart, so it is an artery. Pupils justify with a route rather than merely voting.

slides.title: State what the calculation cannot show
body: Warm-up N has greater volume output than M.
Does that alone prove a person is healthier?
slides.notes: No. These are constructed records; health, demand and oxygen content are not measured. Keep the conclusion to the supplied output comparison.

slides.title: Before you begin
body: Which practice will give a useful record of learning?
slides.notes: Correct: answer independently with agreed support recorded; review afterwards. Read the support record aloud if needed.

options.text: Record the route and support; answer first; use feedback afterwards.
options.feedback: That makes the evidence interpretable and keeps feedback separate from the attempt.

options.text: Convert the total directly into a predicted GCSE grade.
options.feedback: Twenty marks of selected teacher-authored content cannot establish an official grade.

options.text: Copy the worked answers while completing the checkpoint.
options.feedback: That would hide which ideas the pupil can currently apply.

slides.title: Set up your selected checkpoint route
body: Use the shared source page and Q1–Q5.
All routes have the same 20 core marks.
slides.notes: Explain calculator and read-aloud access. Write the route/support on the feedback page before timing begins. Do not impose a penalty for the route choice.

slides.title: Independent checkpoint: 18 minutes
body: Answer Q1–Q5. Show units and causal links.
If stuck, move on and return.
slides.notes: Keep answer reveals closed. Offer agreed access support without supplying scientific content; record any additional content prompts. Optional challenge audit is unscored and only after the core.

slides.title: Feedback starts now
body: Pause or collect the first attempt.
Use item evidence to choose one correction.
slides.notes: Use the five four-mark item guides. A pupil can mark one selected item while teacher completes the rest after class; do not try to read every model answer aloud in two minutes. Preserve the original response before correction.

slides.title: Audience: identify the next move
body: L1. Share one correction with an adult or partner.
Say which mechanism or calculation it improves.
slides.notes: Accept a quiet conference. Convert “revise everything” into a specific action, such as pressure direction, mL-to-L conversion or hormone versus storage.

slides.title: Finish with a targeted action
body: E1. Name one idea you can now explain.
E2. State one practice that would improve your next attempt.
slides.notes: No new scored science items. Use Q1–Q5 evidence to justify the chosen practice; avoid labelling a pupil by the score.

slides.title: Store the evidence, not a label
body: Keep the attempt, route, support and correction together.
slides.notes: Shared exit minute. Retest with a fresh equivalent item later if useful; do not reuse the same answer as independent evidence.

pupilPages.title: Shared sources | Warm-up and checkpoint
pupilPages.intro: All numbers are constructed classroom records. Warm-up letters M/N are separate from checkpoint letters A/B and U/V.

blocks.text: Warm-up only: M has 60 beats/min and 50 mL/beat; N has 80 beats/min and 50 mL/beat. W1 calculate N. W2 test “all hormones affect every cell equally”. W3 classify a pulmonary artery using direction.
Pump output = heart rate × stroke volume. 1,000 mL = 1 L. The table does not measure health or fitness.
Idealised relative index = area × concentration difference ÷ thickness, with the same omitted constant. These are model inputs, not measured human gas-exchange data.
Q1 context: glucose absorption has raised blood glucose. Q2 starts with oxygenated blood leaving the lungs. Q4 concerns quiet inhalation and oxygen exchange into arriving blood.

pupilPages.title: Supported checkpoint | 20 core marks
pupilPages.intro: Same concepts and marks. Optional word bank: pancreas; liver; insulin; glycogen; atrium; ventricle; aorta. Record support used.

blocks.prompt: Q1 [4 marks]. Blood glucose has risen after glucose absorption. Name the gland and hormone involved, describe one target-tissue response, and state its effect on blood glucose. Use four short points.
Q2 [4 marks]. Complete: lungs → [chamber] → [chamber] → [large artery] → body. Then define an artery by direction.
Q3 [4 marks]. Use record A. Show the pump-output calculation in mL/min, convert to L/min, and explain why heart rate alone cannot always compare output.
Q4 [4 marks]. During inhalation, state the volume change and pressure change. Explain the direction of oxygen diffusion at an alveolus and why a thin barrier helps. Link each feature to its effect.
Q5 [4 marks]. Compare U and V: identify the changed factor, calculate V’s index, compare V’s index with U’s, and state one limit of this model.

pupilPages.title: Feedback and next step | Keep the first attempt
pupilPages.intro: Complete after the independent checkpoint. This is a selected-topic check, not a GCSE grade.

blocks.prompt: Record: route used; calculator; read-aloud; any content prompts or additional support.
Total /20: ____ . L1. Preserve your first answer; write one correction and explain the scientific reason.
E1. One idea I can explain now. E2. One precise practice for my next attempt.

answers.label: Retrieval, We do and hinge
answers.answer: R1 blood. R2 ventilation moves air; diffusion is net particle movement down a concentration gradient. W1 M = 3,000 mL/min = 3 L/min; N = 4,000 mL/min = 4 L/min. W2 target-cell recognition/responsiveness matters. W3 pulmonary artery is an artery because it leaves the heart. Output alone does not establish health. Correct hinge: record support, attempt first and review afterwards.

answers.label: Q1: 4 marks, same across all routes
answers.answer: Award one mark each: pancreas [1]; insulin [1]; one valid response such as increased glucose uptake in responsive tissues or increased glycogen storage in liver/muscle [1]; blood glucose decreases towards its usual range [1]. Do not require beta-cell terminology. Do not credit insulin becoming glycogen. Some glucose uptake is insulin-independent.

answers.label: Q2: 4 marks, same across all routes
answers.answer: Lungs → left atrium [1] → left ventricle [1] → aorta [1] → body. Artery carries blood away from the heart [1]. Accept LA/LV if meaning is clear. Oxygen-rich is not a sufficient definition; pulmonary artery is the counterexample.

answers.label: Q3: 4 marks, same across all routes
answers.answer: A: 75 × 80 [1] = 6,000 mL/min [1]; 6 L/min [1]; output also depends on stroke volume, so heart rate alone is insufficient [1]. Accept consistent error-carried-forward for the conversion method if a previous arithmetic slip occurred. If B is used as evidence: 100 × 50 = 5,000 mL/min = 5 L/min, despite its higher heart rate. A correct unsupported final 6 L/min can receive the result and conversion marks, but not the explicit-working mark.

answers.label: Q4: 4 marks, same across all routes
answers.answer: Thoracic volume increases [1]; pressure falls below atmospheric/surrounding air pressure [1]; oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into arriving blood down its concentration gradient [1]; a thin barrier shortens diffusion distance [1]. For the third mark require direction and gradient. Cellular respiration and ventilation alone do not name the exchange mechanism.

answers.label: Q5: 4 marks, same across all routes
answers.answer: Thickness changes, from 1 to 2 [1]. V = 4 × 3 / 2 = 6 [1]. U = 12, so V has half U’s index [1]. One specific limit [1]: relative uncalibrated inputs, omitted proportionality/diffusion coefficient, uniform fixed barrier/concentration difference, no changing blood flow or ventilation, or no tissue-demand information. Do not accept only “it is a model” without explaining the limitation. Allow consistent comparison reasoning after an arithmetic slip; do not award two marks for one unexplained value.

answers.label: Optional unscored audit
answers.answer: A defensible answer identifies oxygen content, distribution to the relevant tissue, exchange effectiveness and/or tissue oxygen demand as additional evidence. Explain why a volume per minute alone cannot show oxygen adequacy. Do not use this answer to add marks to the 20-mark core.

answers.label: Marking and feedback
answers.answer: Five items × four marks = 20. Record route and support separately from marks; scores from different support conditions are not directly interchangeable. This small checkpoint has no official grade boundaries. Use item evidence: Q1 signal/response reteach; Q2 trace left-heart route; Q3 units and multiplication; Q4 volume/pressure and gradient; Q5 controlled factors and model scope.

answers.label: L1 and exit
answers.answer: Accept a specific correction tied to an item and a scientific reason. E1 names a demonstrable idea; E2 identifies a concrete practice, such as a fresh mL-to-L calculation or annotating a pressure sequence. Generic confidence alone is not the intended evidence.

teacherNotes: 40-minute lesson. Zero-minute slides share the preceding stage allocation.
Choose one response route. Accept accurate speech, pointing with explanation, annotations or writing; record the support used.
A teacher or TA can be a quiet audience: ask one evidence question, then let the pupil revise or justify a decision.
Assessment sequence: analogous recap and joint examples, then 18 uninterrupted minutes for the selected 20-mark route. Teacher feedback begins only after the first attempt is paused or collected.
The interactive panel uses only warm-up cases M/N and general route principles. It does not reveal checkpoint A/B output, U/V calculations or the Q1–Q5 mark scheme.
Give focused feedback to one chosen item during the three-minute review and complete any remaining marking afterwards. Preserve original responses and corrections as separate evidence.
Same core concepts and marks across routes. The supported word bank and reading support affect interpretation, so record them; do not assign a fixed attainment identity from a route or score.

steps.question: Why can a hormone carried in blood produce different responses in different cells?

choices.text: Cells differ in whether they recognise and respond to the signal.
choices.feedback: Circulation distributes hormones; target-cell recognition and response matter.

choices.text: Blood delivers every hormone only to a single cell.
choices.feedback: Blood distribution is not a one-cell delivery route.

steps.question: Why is the pulmonary artery an artery?

choices.text: It carries blood away from the heart.
choices.feedback: Direction defines an artery, including the heart-to-lung route.
The pulmonary artery is relatively oxygen-poor; oxygen content does not define the vessel class.

choices.feedback: 80 × 50 = 4,000. Divide mL by 1,000 to obtain litres.
The multiplication is ten times too small. Keep both factors and check the conversion.
